title: Operation Barbarossa
place: The Soviet Union's western borderlands, from the Baltic to the Black Sea

sides.focus: Germany, Romania, Finland, Hungary, Italy and Slovakia

strength.focus: c. 3.3 million German troops, with c. 600,000 allied; c. 3,500 tanks and c. 2,500 aircraft
strength.opponent: c. 2.7–3 million in the western military districts

casualties: Soviet losses in 1941 c. 4.5 million, including c. 3 million captured; German c. 800,000 casualties by the end of November
summary: At dawn on 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies invade the Soviet Union along an 1,800-mile front, opening the largest and most murderous campaign in history.
detail:
Hitler had long seen the conquest of 'living space' in the east as the core of his war. Three army groups attacked at first light: North towards Leningrad, Centre towards Smolensk and Moscow, South into Ukraine. Romania joined at once; Finland, Hungary, Italy and Slovakia within days. Stalin had dismissed repeated warnings, and the Red Army, half-reorganised and stripped of officers by the purges, was caught forward and unready. Some 1,200 Soviet aircraft were lost on the first day, most on the ground.

The panzer groups drove deep and closed vast encirclements at Białystok and Minsk, Smolensk, Uman and Kiev, taking prisoners by the hundred thousand. Yet Soviet resistance was stubborn from the start, reserves kept appearing, and by August German planners admitted they had badly underestimated their enemy.

Barbarossa was conceived as a war of annihilation. Commissars were to be shot on capture, Soviet prisoners were left to starve, the Hunger Plan anticipated the death of millions of civilians, and behind the front the Einsatzgruppen began the mass murder of Soviet Jews.
significance: The invasion turned the war into a struggle for existence on the Eastern Front, where the bulk of the German army would be fought and destroyed, and it opened the way to the Holocaust as systematic mass murder.
uncertaintyNote: Strength and loss figures depend on what is counted (allied contingents, rear services, the period covered); the totals given are commonly cited ranges, the Soviet ones drawn largely from Krivosheev's figures.
sources: David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
David Stahel, Operation Barbarossa and Germany's Defeat in the East (2009)
Richard Overy, Russia's War (1997)
Gerhard Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)

title: Defence of the Brest Fortress
place: Brest-Litovsk fortress, on the Bug (Brest, Belarus)
casualties: German 45th Infantry Division c. 450 killed and c. 1,000 wounded; Soviet c. 2,000 or more killed and several thousand captured
summary: On the frontier itself, the garrison of the old Tsarist fortress at Brest fights on for days after the front has rolled past, its last defenders holding out into July.
detail:
The nineteenth-century citadel at Brest stood on islands where the Bug and Mukhavets meet, directly on the new German–Soviet border. At 4.15 on the morning of 22 June German artillery and heavy mortars opened fire, and the Austrian 45th Infantry Division stormed across the river expecting to take the fortress in hours. Several thousand Soviet soldiers, frontier guards and NKVD troops, many with their families, were trapped inside.

The defenders, fragmented and leaderless at first, fought from barracks, casemates and cellars. Organised resistance in most sectors ended within a week, after the Germans brought up siege mortars and heavy bombs. Small groups held out much longer, short of water and ammunition; Major Pyotr Gavrilov, wounded, was captured only on 23 July. Commissar Fomin was shot after capture under the Commissar Order.

The 45th Division lost more men at Brest than it had in the whole of the campaign in France.
significance: Brest became one of the founding legends of Soviet wartime memory, a sign that the Red Army could fight even in the chaos of June 1941, though it barely delayed the German advance.
uncertaintyNote: The date when the last resistance ended is uncertain; Soviet accounts long told of defenders surviving into August, and some details of the legend cannot be verified. Garrison and loss figures vary between sources.
sources: Rostislav Aliev, The Siege of Brest 1941 (2013)
Richard Overy, Russia's War (1997)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)

title: Battle of Białystok–Minsk
place: Between Białystok and Minsk, Belorussia (Poland and Belarus)
casualties: Soviet Western Front c. 420,000 killed, missing or captured (Germans claimed c. 320,000 prisoners); German losses far lower
summary: Army Group Centre's two panzer groups race around the Soviet Western Front and meet at Minsk, trapping hundreds of thousands of Red Army soldiers in the first great encirclement of the war.
detail:
The Soviet Western Front under General Dmitry Pavlov was packed into the Białystok salient, which bulged into German-occupied Poland. From 22 June Guderian's 2nd Panzer Group swept round its southern flank and Hoth's 3rd Panzer Group round its northern one, while infantry armies pressed in behind. Soviet counter-attacks by mechanised corps, launched on Moscow's orders without fuel, air cover or coordination, were shattered.

The panzer pincers met near Minsk, the Belorussian capital, which fell on 28 June. Inside the double pocket around Białystok, Novogrudok and Minsk, trapped divisions tried to break out east through forests and marshes; many men escaped in small groups, many more were killed or marched into captivity. Resistance in the pocket ended around 9 July.

Stalin had Pavlov and several of his generals arrested and shot for the collapse, a scapegoating of commanders who had been given impossible orders.
significance: In under three weeks the main Soviet force covering Moscow was destroyed, opening the road to Smolensk and convincing Hitler and his generals that the campaign was all but won.
uncertaintyNote: German prisoner claims and Soviet loss figures do not match exactly; the Soviet figure given is Krivosheev's total of irrecoverable losses for the Western Front over the period.
sources: David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
G. F. Krivosheev, ed., Soviet Casualties and Combat Losses in the Twentieth Century (1997)
David Stahel, Operation Barbarossa and Germany's Defeat in the East (2009)

title: Einsatzgruppen and the Holocaust by bullets
place: German-occupied Soviet territory, from the Baltic states to Ukraine

sides.focus: Germany (SS, police and army), with local auxiliaries and Romanian forces
sides.opponent: Jews of the occupied Soviet Union, with Roma, Soviet officials and others

casualties: c. 1.5–2 million Jews murdered by shooting in the occupied Soviet territories, most of them in 1941–42
summary: Behind the advancing armies, SS Einsatzgruppen, police battalions and local collaborators shoot Jewish men, then whole communities, at pits on the edge of hundreds of towns.
detail:
Four Einsatzgruppen, lettered A to D and some 3,000 men in all, followed the army groups into Soviet territory with orders to kill Communist officials and 'Jews in party and state positions'. They were joined by Order Police battalions, Waffen-SS brigades and local auxiliaries, and supplied and often assisted by the Wehrmacht. In Lithuania, Latvia and western Ukraine, pogroms broke out in the first days.

From late July 1941 the killing widened to women and children, and in late August some 23,600 Jews were shot over three days at Kamianets-Podilskyi. Babi Yar, Rumbula, Ponary and the Ninth Fort at Kaunas followed. The method was everywhere the same: victims were marched out of town, made to undress and shot at ravines or freshly dug pits, often in front of local people.

By the end of 1941 the units reported several hundred thousand dead. Massacres went on through 1942 and 1943 as surviving ghettos were liquidated, and Soviet prisoners, Roma and psychiatric patients were also murdered.
significance: The mass shootings marked the transition from persecution to the physical annihilation of European Jewry, months before the death camps began their work, and they claimed roughly a quarter of all Holocaust victims.
uncertaintyNote: Totals rest on the Einsatzgruppen's own incident reports, post-war trials and Soviet commissions; estimates for all shooting victims range from about 1.5 to over 2 million. The radius marks the main killing zone only.
sources: Christopher Browning, The Origins of the Final Solution (2004)
Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (3rd edn, 2003)
Timothy Snyder, Bloodlands (2010)
Patrick Desbois, The Holocaust by Bullets (2008)

title: Ponary massacres
place: Ponary forest, near Wilno (Paneriai, Vilnius, Lithuania)

sides.focus: Germany (SD and Einsatzkommando 9), with the Lithuanian Special Squad
sides.opponent: Jews of Wilno, with Poles and Soviet prisoners of war

casualties: c. 70,000–100,000 people murdered, of whom c. 70,000 were Jews
summary: In the woods outside Wilno, German SD men and a Lithuanian killing squad shoot tens of thousands of Jews at pits the Soviets had dug for fuel tanks.
detail:
Wilno, the 'Jerusalem of Lithuania', had one of the great Jewish communities of Europe, some 60,000 strong in 1941. When German troops arrived in late June, the Security Police set up a squad of Lithuanian volunteers, the Ypatingasis būrys, to do the killing under German direction. Ponary, a wooded spot on the railway a few miles out of the city, had large pits dug by the Soviets for an oil depot.

From July 1941 Jews seized in the streets, then whole groups taken from the city and later from the ghetto, were marched or driven there and shot. By the end of 1941 most of Wilno's Jews were dead. Killing at Ponary continued until the eve of the Red Army's return in July 1944, and Polish prisoners and Soviet captives died there too.

A Polish journalist who lived nearby, Kazimierz Sakowicz, secretly recorded what he saw in a diary he buried in bottles; he was killed in 1944. In 1943–44 a prisoner work detail was forced to exhume and burn the bodies to hide the crime.
significance: Ponary was one of the largest killing sites of the Holocaust by bullets and destroyed the heart of Lithuanian Jewry; the ghetto underground's knowledge of it fed the call to resistance in Wilno.
uncertaintyNote: Total figures for Ponary vary between about 70,000 and 100,000; the Jewish share is the most firmly established. The killings began in early July 1941; exact first dates differ in accounts.
sources: Yitzhak Arad, Ghetto in Flames (1980)
Kazimierz Sakowicz, Ponary Diary, 1941–1943 (2005)
Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (3rd edn, 2003)

title: Mass death of Soviet prisoners of war
place: Prisoner camps in the occupied Soviet Union, Poland and Germany
casualties: c. 3 million of c. 5.7 million Soviet prisoners died in German hands; c. 2 million of them by February 1942
summary: Millions of captured Red Army soldiers are herded into open-air enclosures and left to die of hunger, cold and disease; political officers and Jews among them are shot.
detail:
The Wehrmacht took more than 3 million prisoners in 1941 and had planned to feed almost none of them. German leaders expected to strip the occupied east of food for the Reich, and the Commissar Order of June 1941 marked political officers for execution on capture.

Captives were marched hundreds of miles, those who fell behind being shot, and penned in barbed-wire enclosures with little or no shelter. Rations were set below survival level. Through the autumn and winter of 1941 they died by the thousand each day from starvation, typhus and exposure; there were reports of cannibalism. Jews, commissars and 'Asiatics' were picked out by SS screening teams and shot. Soviet prisoners were the first victims of experimental gassings with Zyklon B at Auschwitz in September 1941.

Only in 1942, when the Reich needed their labour, did conditions improve slightly. Survivors who returned home after 1945 were often treated with suspicion by the Soviet state.
significance: After the murder of the Jews, the killing of Soviet prisoners was the largest single crime of the Nazi regime, and it was carried out mainly by the regular army.
uncertaintyNote: The total number of prisoners and deaths depends on German and Soviet record-keeping; Streit's estimate of about 3.3 million dead is widely cited, others give 2.5 to 3.3 million. The geometry is indicative only.
sources: Christian Streit, Keine Kameraden (1978)
Timothy Snyder, Bloodlands (2010)
Richard Overy, Blood and Ruins (2021)

title: Battle of Smolensk
place: Smolensk and the upper Dnieper, western Russia
casualties: Soviet c. 760,000, of which c. 485,000 killed, missing or captured; German c. 100,000 or more
summary: Army Group Centre encircles another Soviet army group around Smolensk, on the road to Moscow, but two months of furious counter-attacks slow the German advance for the first time.
detail:
Crossing the Dnieper in early July, Guderian's and Hoth's panzer groups drove past Smolensk on either side; the city fell on 16 July and three Soviet armies were trapped to its west. The pocket was not finally cleared until early August, and the Germans claimed some 300,000 prisoners.

Yet the battle was not another Minsk. Timoshenko threw newly raised armies against the German flanks in a series of clumsy but costly counter-attacks, and German panzer divisions, far ahead of their infantry and supplies, were worn down. Around the salient of Yelnya, Zhukov's Reserve Front fought a bitter positional battle and on 6 September forced the Germans out, the first planned withdrawal of the German army in the war.

At Hitler's headquarters the generals urged an advance on Moscow; Hitler instead turned Guderian's panzer group south into Ukraine and Hoth's north towards Leningrad.
significance: Smolensk cost the Germans time and strength they could not spare, and Hitler's decision to divert his armour to Kiev postponed the drive on Moscow until autumn.
uncertaintyNote: The battle's dates are conventional, following Soviet usage; Soviet figures are Krivosheev's totals for the Smolensk defensive operation. German losses are less precisely established.
sources: David M. Glantz, Barbarossa Derailed: The Battle for Smolensk, vols 1–2 (2010–12)
David Stahel, Operation Barbarossa and Germany's Defeat in the East (2009)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)

title: The Atlantic Charter
place: Placentia Bay, off Argentia, Newfoundland (Canada)
summary: Churchill and Roosevelt meet aboard warships in a Newfoundland bay and set out shared aims for the post-war world, though the United States is still not at war.
detail:
Churchill crossed the Atlantic in the new battleship Prince of Wales, Roosevelt arrived aboard the cruiser Augusta, having told the press he was going fishing. Over four days in Placentia Bay the two leaders, with their military chiefs, met for the first time as heads of government, held a shared Sunday service on the battleship's quarterdeck, and discussed Japan, the Atlantic and aid to Britain and the Soviet Union.

Their joint declaration, published on 14 August, set out eight principles: no territorial gains, no changes of territory against the wishes of the peoples concerned, the right of peoples to choose their own government, freer trade, economic cooperation, freedom from fear and want, freedom of the seas, and the disarmament of aggressors pending a wider system of security.

The Charter promised more than either man meant to deliver. Churchill soon insisted that self-determination did not apply to the British Empire, but colonial nationalists in India, Burma and Africa took it at its word.
significance: The Charter bound a neutral United States publicly to the defeat of Nazism, became the basis of the Declaration by United Nations of 1 January 1942, and was an ancestor of the United Nations itself.
uncertaintyNote: No Axis power was party to the meeting; the 'focus' slot is filled only by the data convention, and the outcome is n/a.
sources: Theodore A. Wilson, The First Summit: Roosevelt and Churchill at Placentia Bay, 1941 (1969)
David Reynolds, The Creation of the Anglo-American Alliance, 1937–41 (1981)
Gerhard Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)

title: The Arctic convoys
place: The Norwegian and Barents Seas, from Iceland and Scotland to Murmansk and Archangel

sides.opponent: Britain, the United States and the Soviet Union

casualties: c. 85 merchant ships and 16 Royal Navy warships lost; c. 3,000 Allied seamen killed
summary: Two months after Barbarossa the first British convoy sails for Archangel, opening a supply route round the North Cape to the Soviet Union through ice, darkness and German attack.
detail:
Convoy Dervish, seven merchant ships with escorts, left Iceland on 21 August 1941 and reached Archangel without loss on 31 August. Regular PQ convoys followed from September, carrying tanks, aircraft, trucks, fuel and raw materials promised by Britain and, under Lend-Lease, by the United States.

The route was among the most dangerous of the war. In winter, polar darkness gave some cover but the ships iced up and seamen faced gales and water that killed in minutes; in summer, endless daylight exposed the convoys to U-boats and bombers from bases in occupied Norway, and to the threat of the battleship Tirpitz lurking in the fjords. The disaster of PQ17 in July 1942 and the Battle of the Barents Sea at the end of that year were still to come.

Some 78 convoys made the run by May 1945, delivering roughly four million tons of cargo.
significance: The convoys were the most visible sign of Western help to the Soviet Union in 1941–42, when it mattered most, though more Lend-Lease supplies eventually travelled via Iran and the Pacific.
uncertaintyNote: Loss totals vary slightly depending on whether ships sunk in port or on return voyages are counted. The ring is indicative of a long sea route, not a single battle; the outcome reflects the convoys' overall success.
sources: Richard Woodman, Arctic Convoys 1941–1945 (1994)
S. W. Roskill, The War at Sea, vols I–II (HMSO, 1954–56)
Gerhard Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)

title: Kiev encirclement
place: East of Kiev (Kyiv), Ukraine
casualties: Soviet c. 700,000, including c. 615,000 killed, missing or captured (Germans claimed c. 665,000 prisoners); German c. 100,000
summary: Guderian's panzers drive south and Kleist's north to meet behind Kiev, destroying the Soviet Southwestern Front in the largest encirclement in military history.
detail:
In late August Hitler, overriding his generals, sent Guderian's panzer group south from the Moscow axis. Kirponos's Southwestern Front still held a great bulge around Kiev along the Dnieper. Zhukov warned Stalin that it would be cut off and urged that the city be abandoned; Stalin removed him as chief of the general staff and ordered Kiev held.

Guderian drove south through Romny while Kleist's 1st Panzer Group broke out of its bridgehead at Kremenchug on 12 September. The two met around Lokhvitsa on 14–15 September, some 200 kilometres east of Kiev. The city fell on 19 September; permission to withdraw came far too late. Kirponos was killed trying to break out on 20 September, and by 26 September resistance in the pocket had ended.

The prisoners, marched west into open camps, began dying in great numbers that autumn, and German units moved into Kiev with the Jewish population at their mercy.
significance: Kiev was the greatest German victory of the campaign and laid Ukraine open, but it cost a month in which the weather turned, and the drive on Moscow began only on 30 September.
uncertaintyNote: The German claim of 665,000 prisoners included men caught outside the pocket; Krivosheev's figure for the Soviet operation as a whole is c. 616,000 irrecoverable losses. Start date follows Guderian's turn south.
sources: David Stahel, Kiev 1941 (2012)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
G. F. Krivosheev, ed., Soviet Casualties and Combat Losses in the Twentieth Century (1997)

title: Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran
place: Iran, from the Gulf to the Caspian

sides.opponent: Britain and the Commonwealth and the Soviet Union

casualties: Iranian several hundred killed, including many sailors at Khorramshahr; British and Soviet losses light
summary: British and Indian troops from Iraq and the Gulf and Soviet armies from the Caucasus invade neutral Iran, seize its oilfields and railway, and force Reza Shah to abdicate.
detail:
After Barbarossa, Britain and the Soviet Union wanted Iran's oil secure and its Trans-Iranian Railway open as a supply route to Russia. They demanded the expulsion of the German community, whose influence they exaggerated, and when Reza Shah stalled they attacked together at dawn on 25 August 1941.

British and Indian forces landed at Abadan and Bandar Shahpur, sinking much of Iran's small navy at Khorramshahr, where its commander was killed, and advanced through the Paytak Pass towards Kermanshah; the 10th Indian Division under William Slim was among them. Soviet columns crossed into Azerbaijan and Gilan in the north. Iran's army collapsed within days and the government ordered a ceasefire on 28 August.

Reza Shah abdicated in favour of his son Mohammad Reza on 16 September, and the Allies entered Tehran the next day. The country stayed under occupation until after the war, and its people suffered food shortages as the occupiers commandeered transport.
significance: The invasion opened the Persian Corridor, through which a large share of Western aid to the Soviet Union was to pass, and set the stage for post-war crises over Soviet influence in northern Iran.
uncertaintyNote: Iran was neutral, not an Axis power; it occupies the 'focus' slot only by the data convention, and 'defeat' here means the Allied side prevailed. Casualty figures are poorly recorded. Iran was neutral, not an Axis power, so the pin is grey rather than coloured as an Axis defeat.
sources: Richard A. Stewart, Sunrise at Abadan: The British and Soviet Invasion of Iran, 1941 (1988)
Gerhard Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)
Ervand Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

title: Siege of Leningrad

markers.name: Road of Life across Lake Ladoga

place: Leningrad (St Petersburg), Russia
casualties: c. 800,000–1,000,000 civilians dead, most from starvation; Soviet military losses on the Leningrad fronts well over 1 million
summary: German troops cut the last land route to Leningrad and Hitler resolves to starve the city rather than storm it. Some 800,000 or more civilians die in a siege of nearly 900 days.
detail:
On 8 September 1941 Army Group North took Shlisselburg on Lake Ladoga, severing the city's land links while Finnish forces closed in from the north. Zhukov was flown in to stiffen the defence and the front held at the city's edge, but Hitler had already decided that Leningrad was to be starved and shelled into extinction, not taken.

In the winter of 1941–42 the bread ration for dependants fell to 125 grams a day, much of it sawdust and other fillers. Without fuel, light or running water, people burned furniture and books, ate wallpaper paste, pets and leather; thousands died each day in the streets and in their flats, and there were cases of cannibalism. From November an ice road across Lake Ladoga, the Road of Life, brought in some food and took out evacuees.

A narrow land corridor was opened in January 1943, and the blockade was finally lifted on 27 January 1944. The city's survival became central to Soviet memory of the war.
significance: Leningrad suffered the greatest loss of life of any modern city under siege; the deliberate starvation of its people was one of the gravest crimes of the German war in the east.
uncertaintyNote: Civilian death estimates vary: the Soviet figure presented at Nuremberg was c. 632,000, while most modern historians suggest 800,000 or more. The whole siege is treated as one event, placed by its start date.
sources: Anna Reid, Leningrad: Tragedy of a City Under Siege, 1941–44 (2011)
David M. Glantz, The Battle for Leningrad, 1941–1944 (2002)
Harrison Salisbury, The 900 Days (1969)

title: Babi Yar
place: Babi Yar ravine, Kiev (Babyn Yar, Kyiv, Ukraine)

sides.focus: Germany (SS and police), with Ukrainian auxiliary police

casualties: 33,771 Jews shot in two days, according to the killers' own report; c. 100,000 people of all origins murdered at the site by 1943
summary: Ten days after Kiev falls, German SS and police units shoot nearly 34,000 of the city's Jews in a ravine on its outskirts over two days, one of the largest single massacres of the Holocaust.
detail:
On 24 September 1941 delayed-action mines left by the NKVD blew up buildings on the Khreshchatyk, Kiev's main street, killing German soldiers and starting fires. The occupiers blamed the Jews. Notices ordered all Jews to assemble on 29 September with documents and warm clothing, and many believed they were to be resettled.

They were led towards the Babi Yar ravine at the city's edge, made to hand over their belongings, undress and lie down in the ravine in rows, and then shot. The killing was carried out by Sonderkommando 4a under Paul Blobel, with Order Police battalions, under the overall command of the Higher SS and Police Leader Friedrich Jeckeln; Ukrainian auxiliaries helped herd the victims, and the Wehrmacht's city command took part in planning.

Babi Yar remained a killing site for two years: Roma, Soviet prisoners, psychiatric patients and Ukrainian nationalists were also murdered there. In 1943 prisoners were forced to exhume and burn the bodies to destroy the evidence.
significance: Babi Yar became a symbol of the Holocaust in the Soviet Union, where for decades official memory refused to name its victims as Jews.
uncertaintyNote: The figure of 33,771 comes from Einsatzgruppe C's operational report; the total for all victims at the site to 1943 is less precise, usually given as 70,000–100,000.
sources: Karel C. Berkhoff, Harvest of Despair: Life and Death in Ukraine under Nazi Rule (2004)
Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (3rd edn, 2003)
Timothy Snyder, Bloodlands (2010)

title: Operation Typhoon: Vyazma and Bryansk
place: The western approaches to Moscow, from Vyazma and Bryansk to the city's outskirts
casualties: Soviet c. 1 million in October alone, including c. 600,000–670,000 prisoners in the Vyazma and Bryansk pockets; German casualties heavy but far smaller
summary: Germany launches its offensive on Moscow, trapping huge Soviet forces at Vyazma and Bryansk, then grinds through mud and frost to within sight of the capital before stalling.
detail:
Guderian struck first on 30 September, the other armies on 2 October. Within a week three panzer groups had closed two great pockets, at Vyazma and Bryansk, around most of three Soviet fronts. Hundreds of thousands were captured and the road to Moscow lay briefly open. Stalin recalled Zhukov from Leningrad to rebuild the defence on the Mozhaisk line.

On 16 October panic swept Moscow: government departments and foreign embassies were evacuated to Kuibyshev, and crowds looted shops. Stalin stayed, and on 7 November held the anniversary parade in Red Square, the troops marching straight to the front. The autumn rains turned roads to mud and the Germans' advance slowed as the pockets were cleared.

When the ground froze in mid-November the offensive resumed. Panzer spearheads reached the Moscow–Volga canal and Krasnaya Polyana, some 30 kilometres from the Kremlin, while Guderian failed to take Tula. In temperatures falling far below zero, with men in summer uniforms and engines that would not start, the attack died at the beginning of December.
significance: Typhoon came close to success but exhausted the German army before Moscow, setting the stage for the Soviet counter-offensive and the failure of Hitler's plan to win in a single campaign.
uncertaintyNote: Prisoner figures for Vyazma and Bryansk are German claims; Soviet totals are Krivosheev's estimates for the defensive operations. The event covers the whole German advance on Moscow from 30 September to 5 December.
sources: David Stahel, Operation Typhoon: Hitler's March on Moscow (2013)
Rodric Braithwaite, Moscow 1941 (2006)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)

title: Odessa massacre
place: Odessa (Odesa, Ukraine) and the village of Dalnik

sides.focus: Romania (army and gendarmerie), with German Sonderkommando 11b

casualties: c. 25,000–34,000 Jews murdered, with further thousands deported to die in Transnistria
summary: After a bomb destroys the Romanian headquarters in newly captured Odessa, Romanian troops take savage reprisals, shooting, hanging and burning alive tens of thousands of the city's Jews.
detail:
Romanian forces had besieged Odessa from August, at great cost, until the Soviets evacuated the port by sea in mid-October. On 22 October 1941 a delayed-action charge left by Soviet engineers blew up the former NKVD building used as Romanian headquarters, killing the city commander, General Ion Glogojeanu, and scores of officers.

On Marshal Antonescu's orders, reprisals followed at once. Thousands of people, most of them Jews, were hanged in the streets or shot. The next day many thousands more were marched out to Dalnik, where some were shot at anti-tank ditches and others locked into warehouses that were set alight or blown up. German Sonderkommando 11b took part in the killing in Odessa.

The survivors were confined in a ghetto and through the winter deported to camps in Transnistria, the Romanian-run zone between the Dniester and the Bug, where tens of thousands more died of cold, hunger and shooting at Bogdanovka and elsewhere.
significance: The Odessa massacre was the worst single atrocity of Romania's war and showed that Germany's allies carried out mass murder on their own initiative; Antonescu was tried and executed in 1946.
uncertaintyNote: Victim numbers vary from about 25,000 to 34,000 for the October killings; the Wiesel Commission's report gives the higher range for those murdered in and near the city.
sources: Radu Ioanid, The Holocaust in Romania (2000)
International Commission on the Holocaust in Romania, Final Report (2004)
Vladimir Solonari, A Satellite Empire: Romanian Rule in Southwestern Ukraine, 1941–1944 (2019)

title: Siege of Sevastopol
place: Sevastopol, Crimea
casualties: Soviet c. 200,000 killed, wounded or captured over the whole siege, with c. 95,000 captured in July 1942; German and Romanian c. 75,000 or more
summary: Manstein's 11th Army overruns Crimea but cannot take the naval fortress of Sevastopol, which holds out for eight months until a final assault with the heaviest guns ever built.
detail:
Breaking through the Perekop isthmus in late October 1941, Manstein's army swept across Crimea, but the Soviet Coastal Army fell back into the ring of forts around Sevastopol, home of the Black Sea Fleet. A first attack in November failed. A second, launched in December, was called off when Soviet troops landed at Kerch and Feodosiya on 26 December, threatening the German rear.

Through the spring of 1942 the city was supplied by sea and its people lived in caves and cellars. In May Manstein destroyed the Soviet Crimean Front on the Kerch peninsula, then turned on Sevastopol. From 2 June an enormous bombardment, including the 800 mm railway gun Dora and massed air attacks, pounded the forts; the infantry attacked on 7 June and took them one by one in desperate fighting.

Senior commanders were evacuated by submarine and aircraft at the end of June, leaving tens of thousands of men to be captured when organised resistance ended on 4 July.
significance: Sevastopol's long defence tied down an entire German army through the first half of 1942, and its fall secured Crimea for the summer offensive towards the Caucasus.
uncertaintyNote: Loss figures for the eight-month siege vary widely between sources. The end date marks the end of organised resistance; scattered fighting went on for some days afterwards.
sources: Robert Forczyk, Where the Iron Crosses Grow: The Crimea 1941–44 (2014)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
Erich von Manstein, Lost Victories (1958)

title: Operation Crusader
place: Eastern Cyrenaica, between Tobruk and the Egyptian frontier, Libya
casualties: Axis c. 38,000 killed, wounded or captured; British and Commonwealth c. 18,000
summary: Eighth Army attacks in the Western Desert to relieve besieged Tobruk. After weeks of confused tank battles around Sidi Rezegh, Rommel is forced back across Cyrenaica.
detail:
Auchinleck's offensive began on 18 November 1941 with the newly named Eighth Army sweeping round the Axis frontier positions towards Tobruk, held since April by Australian, then British, Polish and Czechoslovak troops. Around the airfield and escarpment at Sidi Rezegh, British armour was committed piecemeal and badly mauled by the Afrika Korps and Italian armoured divisions; the South African 5th Brigade was overrun on 23 November.

Rommel then gambled on a 'dash to the wire', driving his panzers towards the Egyptian frontier to unhinge the enemy. Cunningham wanted to break off; Auchinleck replaced him with Ritchie and ordered the battle continued. Rommel's raid ran out of fuel, New Zealand troops broke through to Tobruk, and short of supplies and tanks, he withdrew in early December, first to Gazala and then to El Agheila. The frontier garrisons at Bardia and Halfaya surrendered in January.

Within weeks Rommel, reinforced, counter-attacked and retook much of the ground.
significance: Crusader was the first British victory over German ground forces in the war and relieved Tobruk, but it did not destroy Rommel's army, and the desert seesaw continued.
uncertaintyNote: Casualty figures vary between British and German sources; the Axis total includes the frontier garrisons captured in January 1942. Strength and tank figures are approximate.
sources: Niall Barr, Pendulum of War: The Three Battles of El Alamein (2004)
I. S. O. Playfair, The Mediterranean and Middle East, vol. III (HMSO, 1960)
Gerhard Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)

title: Battle of Moscow: the Soviet counter-offensive
place: North, west and south of Moscow
casualties: Soviet c. 370,000, including c. 140,000 killed or missing; German several hundred thousand over the winter, including frostbite cases
summary: With German troops frozen in front of Moscow, fresh Soviet armies strike back in deep snow, driving the invaders back up to 250 kilometres and ending the hope of a quick German victory.
detail:
On 5 December 1941 Konev's Kalinin Front attacked north of Moscow, and the next day Zhukov's Western Front and the right wing of the Southwestern Front joined in. Stalin had husbanded reserves, including divisions brought from Siberia and the Far East after intelligence suggested Japan would not attack the Soviet Union, and newly raised armies. In temperatures of thirty degrees below zero and worse, ski troops and cavalry got behind exhausted German units whose vehicles and weapons froze.

Klin and Kalinin were retaken in mid-December, the threat to Tula was lifted, and the Germans abandoned guns and vehicles as they fell back. Hitler forbade retreat, sacked Brauchitsch and took personal command of the army, and dismissed Guderian, Hoepner and dozens of other generals. His order to stand fast may have prevented a rout, at terrible cost.

In January Stalin, over-confident, widened the offensive along the whole front; it gained ground but failed to destroy Army Group Centre, and petered out by April.
significance: The battle of Moscow was Germany's first major defeat of the war: the Blitzkrieg against the Soviet Union had failed, and Germany now faced a long war on several fronts, just as the United States entered it.
uncertaintyNote: Soviet figures are Krivosheev's for the Moscow offensive operation to 7 January 1942; German winter losses are hard to separate from sickness and frostbite. Its start on 5 December falls just before the 'pacific' phase boundary.
sources: Rodric Braithwaite, Moscow 1941 (2006)
David Stahel, The Battle for Moscow (2015)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
place: Pearl Harbor, Oahu, Hawaii

strength.focus: 6 carriers, 353 aircraft in two waves, 5 midget submarines
strength.opponent: 8 battleships in harbour; c. 390 aircraft on Oahu

casualties: American 2,403 killed, including 68 civilians, and c. 1,178 wounded; 8 battleships damaged, of which Arizona and Oklahoma were total losses; c. 180 aircraft destroyed. Japanese 64 killed, 29 aircraft lost
summary: On a Sunday morning, aircraft from six Japanese carriers strike the US Pacific Fleet at anchor at Pearl Harbor, sinking or crippling its battleships and bringing the United States into the war.
detail:
Admiral Yamamoto's plan was to knock out the Pacific Fleet while Japan seized the oil and rubber of South-East Asia. Nagumo's carrier force crossed the North Pacific in radio silence, and at 7.55 local time on 7 December 1941 the first of two waves, led by Mitsuo Fuchida, fell on the fleet and the airfields of Oahu. Warnings, including a radar sighting, had been missed or dismissed, and Japan's note breaking off negotiations was delivered in Washington only after the attack had begun.

Torpedo planes and bombers struck Battleship Row. Arizona blew up when a bomb set off her forward magazine, killing 1,177 of her crew; Oklahoma capsized. Aircraft were destroyed in rows on the ground. In under two hours the battle fleet was out of action.

But the American carriers were at sea, and the oil tanks, dockyards and submarine base were left largely untouched. Most of the damaged battleships were raised and returned to service.
significance: Pearl Harbor united a divided America behind war; Roosevelt called it 'a date which will live in infamy', and within days the conflicts in Europe and Asia had merged into a world war.
uncertaintyNote: The attack began just before 8 a.m. on 7 December in Hawaii, already 8 December in Tokyo; landings in Malaya had begun an hour or so earlier in absolute time. Aircraft loss figures vary slightly by source.
sources: Gordon W. Prange, At Dawn We Slept (1981)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
Jonathan Parshall and Anthony Tully, Shattered Sword (2005)
Gerhard Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)

title: Japanese invasion of Malaya
place: Southern Thailand and the Malay peninsula (Malaysia)
casualties: British, Indian, Australian and Malay forces c. 50,000 killed, wounded or captured before Singapore; Japanese c. 4,600
summary: Japanese troops land in southern Thailand and northern Malaya and in eight weeks drive the larger British and Commonwealth army down the length of the peninsula to Singapore.
detail:
Just after midnight on 8 December 1941 local time, before the attack on Pearl Harbor, the 25th Army under Yamashita Tomoyuki began landing at Kota Bharu in Malaya and at Singora and Patani in Thailand. The RAF's northern airfields were quickly overrun or abandoned, and on 10 December Japanese aircraft sank the British capital ships sent to stop the landings.

Yamashita's three divisions were experienced and well led, with tanks and command of the air; his opponents, Indian, British, Australian and local troops, were often raw and road-bound. Again and again the Japanese outflanked defensive positions through jungle and rubber plantations, by bicycle and by small landings along the coast. Defeats at Jitra in December and Slim River on 7 January broke the 11th Indian Division; Kuala Lumpur fell on 11 January. Australians fought hard at Gemas and Muar, but the retreat continued.

On 31 January the last troops crossed the causeway to Singapore island and it was blown behind them. Malaya's tin and rubber were in Japanese hands.
significance: The speed of the Malayan campaign shattered the myth of British power in Asia and placed Singapore, the keystone of imperial defence in the east, under direct siege.
uncertaintyNote: Allied losses before Singapore are approximate, as many men were cut off and captured in small groups. The Kota Bharu landings preceded Pearl Harbor by about an hour in absolute time.
sources: Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)
Alan Warren, Singapore 1942: Britain's Greatest Defeat (2002)
Brian P. Farrell, The Defence and Fall of Singapore 1940–1942 (2005)

title: Sinking of Prince of Wales and Repulse
place: South China Sea, off Kuantan, Malaya

strength.focus: c. 85 land-based bombers and torpedo bombers

casualties: British 840 killed, including Admiral Phillips; Japanese 3 or 4 aircraft lost
summary: Japanese naval bombers flying from Indochina sink the battleship Prince of Wales and the battlecruiser Repulse at sea, leaving Britain with no capital ships in the Far East.
detail:
Prince of Wales and Repulse had reached Singapore on 2 December as 'Force Z', sent by Churchill to deter Japan. On 8 December Admiral Tom Phillips sailed north to attack the invasion convoys off Kota Bharu, without fighter cover. Spotted and having lost the element of surprise, he turned back, then diverted towards a false report of landings at Kuantan.

On the morning of 10 December, waves of high-level bombers and torpedo bombers of the navy's 22nd Air Flotilla, flying from bases around Saigon, found the ships. Torpedoes jammed the battleship's port propeller shaft and flooded her; Repulse, skilfully handled, dodged many attacks before she too was hit repeatedly and sank. Prince of Wales went down less than an hour later. Destroyers picked up more than 2,000 survivors; Phillips was not among them.
significance: It was the first time capital ships under way had been sunk by aircraft alone, confirming the end of the battleship era and leaving Malaya and the Indian Ocean exposed.
uncertaintyNote: The two wrecks lie a few miles apart; the position given is between them.
sources: Martin Middlebrook and Patrick Mahoney, Battleship: The Loss of the Prince of Wales and the Repulse (1977)
Arthur J. Marder, Old Friends, New Enemies, vol. I (1981)
Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)

title: Battle of Hong Kong

markers.name: Shing Mun Redoubt, Gin Drinkers Line

place: Kowloon and Hong Kong Island
casualties: Allied c. 1,500–2,100 killed and c. 10,000 captured; Japanese c. 2,000–2,700 killed or wounded; many civilians
summary: A small garrison of British, Canadian, Indian and local troops holds Hong Kong for seventeen days against a Japanese division before surrendering on Christmas Day.
detail:
Hours after Pearl Harbor, Japanese aircraft destroyed the colony's few planes at Kai Tak and the 38th Division crossed the border from China. The Gin Drinkers Line, meant to hold for weeks, was broken when the Shing Mun Redoubt fell on the night of 9–10 December, and General Maltby withdrew his men from Kowloon to the island.

On the night of 18 December the Japanese landed on the north shore of Hong Kong Island. The Canadians of the Winnipeg Grenadiers and Royal Rifles, newly arrived and barely trained, fought with Indian battalions, the Middlesex and the Hong Kong Volunteer Defence Corps in the hills, losing the key Wong Nai Chung Gap, where the Canadian brigadier Lawson was killed. Cut off from water reservoirs and split in two, the garrison surrendered on 25 December.

Captured soldiers and medical staff were murdered at the Salesian Mission and at St Stephen's College, where wounded men were bayoneted in their beds and nurses raped and killed.
significance: The fall of Hong Kong was the first surrender of a British colony to Japan and began nearly four years of occupation, during which the population fell by more than half through flight, hunger and terror.
uncertaintyNote: Japanese strength and casualty figures, and Allied killed totals, vary considerably between sources.
sources: Philip Snow, The Fall of Hong Kong (2003)
Tony Banham, Not the Slightest Chance: The Defence of Hong Kong, 1941 (2003)
Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)

title: The Philippines, Bataan and the Death March
place: Luzon, Philippines
casualties: c. 76,000 Filipino and American troops surrendered on Bataan; on the Death March c. 500–650 Americans and c. 5,000–18,000 Filipinos died, and many thousands more in Camp O'Donnell
summary: Japan wrecks MacArthur's air force and invades Luzon. Filipino and American troops hold out on Bataan for three months, then are driven on a murderous march into captivity.
detail:
On 8 December, some nine hours after Pearl Harbor, Japanese bombers caught most of MacArthur's aircraft on the ground at Clark Field. Homma Masaharu's 14th Army landed at Lingayen Gulf on 22 December, and MacArthur fell back on the pre-war plan: he declared Manila an open city and withdrew his Filipino and American forces into the jungle-covered Bataan peninsula.

On Bataan the defenders repulsed the first Japanese assaults but were cut to half rations, then less, and ravaged by malaria and dysentery. Ordered out by Roosevelt, MacArthur left for Australia in March, promising 'I shall return'. A renewed Japanese offensive broke the line in early April, and on 9 April General Edward King surrendered, the largest capitulation in American military history.

The starving prisoners were driven some 100 kilometres north from Mariveles in tropical heat, then crammed into boxcars to Capas and Camp O'Donnell. Guards beat, bayoneted and shot those who fell or sought water. Thousands died on the march, and many thousands more in the camp in the following weeks, most of them Filipinos.
significance: Bataan delayed Japan's timetable in the Philippines; the Death March became one of the defining atrocities of the Pacific war, and Homma was executed for it in 1946.
uncertaintyNote: Death toll estimates for the march, especially for Filipinos, vary widely because no reliable count was kept. Corregidor, which held out until May, is treated separately.
sources: Louis Morton, The Fall of the Philippines (US Army official history, 1953)
Michael Norman and Elizabeth M. Norman, Tears in the Darkness (2009)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)

title: Battle of Wake Island
place: Wake Island, central Pacific

strength.focus: c. 2,000 landing troops in the second assault, with carrier support
strength.opponent: c. 520 Marines and naval personnel; c. 1,150 civilian contractors

casualties: American c. 120 military and c. 70 civilians killed; c. 1,600 captured. Japanese c. 800–1,000 killed, two destroyers sunk
summary: The small Marine garrison of Wake atoll beats off a Japanese landing on 11 December, sinking two destroyers, before a second assault overwhelms it two weeks later.
detail:
Wake, a remote atoll between Hawaii and Guam, was being built up as an air and submarine base. Japanese bombers from the Marshalls struck on 8 December (local date), destroying most of the newly arrived Marine fighters on the ground. On 11 December an invasion force under Admiral Kajioka closed in, but the Marines' coastal guns held fire until it was in close range, then hit several ships and sank the destroyer Hayate; the remaining Wildcats sank the destroyer Kisaragi. It was one of the very few occasions in the war when an amphibious assault was beaten off by shore defences.

A relief force built around the carrier Saratoga set out from Pearl Harbor but was recalled. Reinforced by two carriers returning from Pearl Harbor, the Japanese landed again before dawn on 23 December and, after hours of close fighting, the island's commander surrendered.

Most prisoners were shipped to China and Japan, but 98 civilian workers were kept on Wake; in October 1943 they were executed on the orders of the island's commander, Sakaibara Shigematsu.
significance: Wake's defence gave Americans a rare story of resistance in the dark first weeks of the war, while its loss cut the route between Hawaii and the Philippines.
uncertaintyNote: Japanese casualty figures vary widely. Dates are local (west of the date line), one day ahead of Hawaii.
sources: Gregory J. W. Urwin, Facing Fearful Odds: The Siege of Wake Island (1997)
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: The Battle for Wake Island (1995)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)

title: Germany declares war on the United States
place: Kroll Opera House (the Reichstag's wartime chamber), Berlin
summary: Four days after Pearl Harbor, Hitler declares war on the United States in a speech to the Reichstag, and Mussolini follows. The European and Pacific wars become one.
detail:
Under the Tripartite Pact Germany was obliged to help Japan only if Japan was attacked, not if it attacked. Yet Hitler, who had promised Tokyo his support, did not hesitate. At the Kroll Opera House on 11 December 1941 he denounced Roosevelt in a long speech, while Ribbentrop handed the American chargé d'affaires a declaration of war. Italy declared war the same afternoon, and Congress replied in kind.

Hitler's reasons have been much debated. The United States was already supplying Britain under Lend-Lease and its navy was escorting convoys and fighting U-boats in an undeclared war; he believed American entry was a matter of time, and that striking first would free his submarines to attack its shipping. He held the United States in contempt as racially mixed and militarily weak and believed Japan would keep it busy in the Pacific. The decision came even as his armies were in retreat before Moscow.
significance: Hitler's declaration resolved Roosevelt's dilemma, allowing him to put the defeat of Germany first, and set the world's greatest industrial power against the Reich.
uncertaintyNote: Motives are a matter of interpretation; this follows the reading of Kershaw, Weinberg and Tooze. The outcome is n/a as a declaration, not a battle.
sources: Ian Kershaw, Fateful Choices (2007)
Gerhard Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)
Adam Tooze, The Wages of Destruction (2006)

title: Third Battle of Changsha
place: Changsha, Hunan, China
casualties: Disputed: Chinese claims of over 50,000 Japanese casualties are generally thought much exaggerated; Japanese records give c. 6,000; Chinese losses also heavy
summary: A Japanese thrust on the Hunan capital is drawn in, surrounded and driven back by Xue Yue's armies, giving Nationalist China a much-needed victory in the dark weeks after Pearl Harbor.
detail:
Changsha, the capital of Hunan and gateway to the rice country south of the Yangzi, had already been attacked by the Japanese 11th Army in 1939 and again in September 1941, when Japanese troops briefly entered the city before withdrawing. At the end of December 1941 General Anami Korechika struck once more, partly to prevent Chinese forces moving south to aid the British at Hong Kong.

Xue Yue, commanding the 9th War Area, used tactics he had refined in the earlier battles: his forces fell back before the Japanese advance across the Xinqiang and Miluo rivers, destroying roads and removing food, while the city's garrison held fast. As the Japanese reached and attacked Changsha in early January, Chinese armies closed in from the flanks and threatened their lines of supply. Anami ordered a withdrawal, which became a costly fighting retreat to the north.

In a period of Allied disasters across Asia, Chongqing trumpeted the battle as a great victory, and it was widely reported in the Allied press.
significance: The third battle of Changsha showed that the Nationalist army could still defeat a major Japanese offensive, and it strengthened China's standing as an ally just as the Pacific war began.
uncertaintyNote: Casualty figures are deeply contested between Chinese and Japanese sources. Changsha was fought over four times (1939, 1941, 1941–42, 1944); this event covers the third battle and mentions the second.
sources: Rana Mitter, China's War with Japan, 1937–1945 (2013)
Mark Peattie, Edward Drea and Hans van de Ven, eds, The Battle for China (2011)
Hsi-sheng Ch'i, Nationalist China at War (1982)

title: Operation Drumbeat
place: Off the east coast of the United States and Canada, later the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean
casualties: c. 400 Allied ships sunk in American waters in the first half of 1942, with several thousand seamen killed; only a handful of U-boats lost
summary: German U-boats strike along the brightly lit American coast, sinking tankers and freighters within sight of shore while the US Navy is slow to adopt convoys.
detail:
Within days of the declaration of war, Dönitz sent five long-range Type IX U-boats across the Atlantic under the code-name Paukenschlag, 'drumbeat'. Operations began on 13 January 1942, though Reinhard Hardegen's U-123 had already sunk the steamer Cyclops off Nova Scotia the day before.

The U-boats found peacetime conditions. Coastal towns were not blacked out, so ships were silhouetted against the lights; merchant vessels sailed alone along predictable routes, and the navy, short of escorts and reluctant to follow British experience, did not introduce coastal convoys until May. Tankers burned off Hatteras and Florida, and bodies and oil washed onto holiday beaches. Further waves of U-boats, supplied at sea by 'milch cow' submarine tankers, extended the hunting into the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean.

German crews called it the second 'happy time'. Only as convoys, air patrols and blackouts spread down the coast in the summer did losses fall, and Dönitz shifted his boats back to the mid-Atlantic.
significance: Drumbeat inflicted the heaviest losses of the Battle of the Atlantic in a few months, threatening fuel supplies to Britain, before American defences caught up and the struggle returned to the convoy routes.
uncertaintyNote: The total ships sunk depends on the area and period counted (the US coast alone, or including the Gulf and Caribbean); about 400 for January–July 1942 is a commonly cited figure.
sources: Michael Gannon, Operation Drumbeat (1990)
Clay Blair, Hitler's U-Boat War: The Hunters, 1939–1942 (1996)
Marc Milner, Battle of the Atlantic (2003)

title: Wannsee Conference
place: Villa at Am Großen Wannsee 56–58, Berlin
summary: Fifteen senior SS officers and civil servants meet over lunch in a lakeside villa to coordinate the deportation and murder of the Jews of Europe, numbered at eleven million.
detail:
Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office, had been charged in July 1941 with preparing a 'total solution of the Jewish question'. He invited state secretaries from the interior, justice and foreign ministries, the Four-Year Plan, the occupied eastern territories and the General Government in Poland, together with senior SS and party officials, to a meeting first set for December and postponed after Pearl Harbor.

By the time they met on 20 January 1942, the mass shootings in the east had killed hundreds of thousands, the gas vans at Chełmno were operating and Bełżec was being built. The meeting did not decide on genocide; it confirmed the SS's control of it and bound the ministries into its execution. Adolf Eichmann's minutes listed some eleven million Jews in every European country, including neutral and enemy states, who were to be 'evacuated to the east', worked to death or 'treated accordingly'. Discussion turned to the status of part-Jews and mixed marriages.

Only one copy of the minutes survived, found by American prosecutors in 1947.
significance: Wannsee laid bare the bureaucratic organisation of the Holocaust: the murder of a continent's Jews coordinated by educated officials as an administrative task.
uncertaintyNote: Historians agree the conference coordinated rather than initiated the Final Solution; the exact timing of the decision for continent-wide murder remains debated.
sources: Mark Roseman, The Villa, the Lake, the Meeting: Wannsee and the Final Solution (2002)
Christopher Browning, The Origins of the Final Solution (2004)
Saul Friedländer, The Years of Extermination (2007)

title: Japanese conquest of Burma
place: Burma (Myanmar), from Tenasserim to the Indian frontier

sides.focus: Japan, with the Burma Independence Army
sides.opponent: Britain and the Commonwealth and China (Nationalist)

casualties: British and Indian c. 13,000 killed, wounded or missing; Chinese losses much heavier; Japanese c. 4,500; tens of thousands of Indian refugees died on the trek to India
summary: Japan's 15th Army drives the British out of Burma in five months, taking Rangoon in March and cutting the Burma Road to China, while hundreds of thousands of Indians flee on foot to India.
detail:
The main Japanese invasion crossed from Thailand on 20 January 1942. Outnumbered and badly trained, the 17th Indian Division was pushed back to the Sittang river, where on 23 February the only bridge was blown with two of its brigades on the far bank. Rangoon, the port through which all supplies for Burma and China came, was evacuated on 7 March and occupied the next day; the new army commander, Harold Alexander, barely escaped encirclement.

Slim took command of Burma Corps and fought a long retreat up the Irrawaddy alongside Chinese armies under Stilwell's nominal direction. A Chinese division under Sun Li-jen helped relieve trapped British troops at the burning Yenangyaung oilfields in April. But Japanese columns took Lashio on 29 April, closing the Burma Road, and Mandalay fell on 1 May. Burma Corps crossed the Chindwin and reached Imphal in mid-May, just before the monsoon.

Some 400,000 or more Indians, Anglo-Burmese and others fled overland, many through malarial mountains; tens of thousands died. The Burma Independence Army marched in with the Japanese, and Burman attacks on Karen and other minorities followed.
significance: The loss of Burma isolated China by land, brought the war to India's frontier, and was the longest retreat in British military history.
uncertaintyNote: Refugee numbers and deaths are estimates ranging widely; Chinese losses in Burma are poorly documented.
sources: Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)
William Slim, Defeat into Victory (1956)
Louis Allen, Burma: The Longest War, 1941–45 (1984)

title: Fall of Singapore

markers.name: Ford factory, site of the surrender

place: Singapore island
casualties: c. 80,000 British, Australian, Indian and local troops captured, adding to c. 50,000 lost in Malaya; Japanese c. 5,000 killed or wounded on the island
summary: A week after crossing the Johore Strait, Yamashita's army forces the surrender of Singapore, Britain's great naval base in the East, with some 80,000 troops passing into captivity.
detail:
On the night of 8 February 1942 Japanese troops crossed the narrow Johore Strait in boats and landed on the north-west coast of Singapore island, held by thinly spread Australian battalions. Within days they had taken the high ground at Bukit Timah and the island's food dumps and reservoirs. The great naval guns, which could fire landward, had few suitable shells; the air force had gone.

Percival's command was confused, his troops disorganised after the retreat, and the city of a million people was swollen with refugees and bombed and shelled daily. On 14 February Japanese soldiers killed patients and staff at the Alexandra Hospital. Facing a collapse of water supplies, Percival met Yamashita at the Ford factory at Bukit Timah on 15 February and agreed to unconditional surrender. Yamashita's own army was short of ammunition.

The prisoners were sent to camps such as Changi and to labour on the Burma–Thailand railway; many Indian soldiers were urged to join the Japanese-sponsored Indian National Army.
significance: Churchill called it the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history. The fall of Singapore destroyed British prestige in Asia and opened the way to the Dutch East Indies.
uncertaintyNote: The number of prisoners taken on the island is variously given as 80,000 to 85,000. The marker for the Ford factory is approximate.
sources: Brian P. Farrell, The Defence and Fall of Singapore 1940–1942 (2005)
Alan Warren, Singapore 1942: Britain's Greatest Defeat (2002)
Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)

title: Sook Ching massacre
place: Singapore, and later across Malaya
casualties: Japanese post-war admission c. 5,000; most historians estimate c. 25,000; Chinese community estimates up to 50,000 or more in Singapore
summary: Days after Singapore falls, the Japanese army screens the island's Chinese men and takes tens of thousands to beaches and plantations to be machine-gunned, in a 'purge through cleansing'.
detail:
The Japanese army regarded the Chinese of Malaya as enemies: many had funded China's war effort, and Chinese volunteers had fought in the defence of Singapore. Three days after the surrender, Chinese men between about 18 and 50 were ordered to assemble at screening centres across the city.

The Kempeitai and army units picked out those they judged hostile, on criteria that were arbitrary in practice: tattoos, spectacles, membership of societies, a teacher's profession, or simply the judgement of a hooded informer. Those selected were taken by lorry to Changi Beach, Punggol, Siglap and other places, roped together and machine-gunned, sometimes at the water's edge so that the sea would carry the bodies away. The operation, known in Chinese as sook ching, was then extended to the Malayan peninsula.

After the war a British military court tried seven officers; Lieutenant-General Kawamura Saburō and Lieutenant-Colonel Ōishi Masayuki were hanged in 1947.
significance: Sook Ching was among the worst atrocities of the Japanese occupation of South-East Asia and remains central to how Singapore remembers the war.
uncertaintyNote: The death toll is unknown and deeply disputed, from the Japanese admission of about 5,000 to Chinese estimates of 50,000 or more; most scholars accept a figure in the tens of thousands.
sources: Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)
Kevin Blackburn and Karl Hack, War Memory and the Making of Modern Malaysia and Singapore (2012)
Kevin Blackburn and Karl Hack, Did Singapore Have to Fall? (2004)

title: Bombing of Darwin
place: Darwin, Northern Territory, Australia

strength.focus: c. 188 carrier aircraft and c. 54 land-based bombers
strength.opponent: a handful of fighters and anti-aircraft guns

casualties: c. 235–250 killed, including civilians and seamen; 8 ships sunk; c. 30 aircraft destroyed. Japanese losses a few aircraft
summary: Aircraft from the carriers that struck Pearl Harbor attack Darwin, sinking ships in the harbour and killing some 240 people in the first and heaviest raid on the Australian mainland.
detail:
Darwin was the main Allied base in northern Australia, crowded with shipping in support of the defence of Timor and Java. On the morning of 19 February 1942 Mitsuo Fuchida led 188 aircraft from four of Nagumo's carriers, stationed in the Timor Sea, against the port. Warnings from coast-watchers and a mission station on Bathurst Island were discounted as returning American fighters.

Bombs and torpedoes sank eight ships in the harbour, among them the US destroyer Peary, and set others ablaze; the wharf was wrecked, with men killed on it. Land-based bombers from Ambon and Kendari then struck the RAAF airfield before noon. Much of the town's population fled south in disorder, and there was looting.

It was the first of some sixty raids on Darwin and northern Australia that continued until late 1943. The Australian government played down the losses at the time.
significance: The raid brought the war to the Australian homeland, deepened fears of invasion and hastened Australia's turn towards the United States for its defence.
uncertaintyNote: The death toll has been given between about 230 and 250; the Lowe Commission of 1942 put it at 243. Japan had no plan to invade Australia, though Australians feared one.
sources: Peter Grose, An Awkward Truth: The Bombing of Darwin, February 1942 (2009)
Douglas Lockwood, Australia's Pearl Harbour (1966)
Jonathan Parshall and Anthony Tully, Shattered Sword (2005)

title: Battle of the Java Sea
place: Java Sea, north of Surabaya, Java (Indonesia)

sides.opponent: Netherlands, Britain, the United States and Australia

casualties: Allied c. 2,300 sailors killed at the Java Sea, more in the actions that followed; 2 cruisers and 3 destroyers sunk on 27 February. Japanese one destroyer damaged
summary: An improvised Allied squadron under the Dutch Admiral Doorman tries to stop the Japanese invasion of Java and is destroyed in a day and night of gunfire and torpedoes.
detail:
By late February 1942 the Japanese had taken Malaya, Borneo, Celebes and Sumatra, and invasion convoys were closing on Java. The Allied ABDA command's remaining ships, Dutch, British, American and Australian, with no common signals or doctrine, put to sea under Rear-Admiral Karel Doorman to attack the eastern convoy.

On the afternoon of 27 February they met its escort under Admiral Takagi. In a long-range gunnery duel HMS Exeter was hit in a boiler room and a Japanese torpedo attack sank the Dutch destroyer Kortenaer. Doorman tried repeatedly to get at the transports. That night, his flagship De Ruyter and the cruiser Java were hit by the formidable Type 93 'Long Lance' torpedoes and sank with heavy loss of life; Doorman went down with his ship.

The survivors tried to escape. Houston and Perth ran into the western invasion force in the Sunda Strait on the night of 28 February and were sunk; Exeter and two destroyers were caught and sunk on 1 March. Java surrendered on 8 March.
significance: The battle destroyed the last Allied naval force in the East Indies and opened Java, with its oil and its 40 million people, to Japanese occupation.
uncertaintyNote: The battle's position is approximate; the main action ranged widely north of Surabaya and Bawean Island. Casualty totals vary depending on whether the Sunda Strait action and 1 March sinkings are included.
sources: H. P. Willmott, Empires in the Balance (1982)
Jeffrey R. Cox, Rising Sun, Falling Skies (2014)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)

title: Operation Reinhard: the death camps
place: Bełżec, Sobibór and Treblinka, in the General Government (eastern Poland)

sides.focus: Germany (SS and police), with Trawniki guards

casualties: c. 1.5–1.7 million Jews murdered in the three camps, with Roma and others
summary: The SS opens Bełżec, then Sobibór and Treblinka, camps built for nothing but killing. In eighteen months some 1.7 million Jews are gassed there, most of them on the day they arrive.
detail:
From the autumn of 1941 the SS and Police Leader in Lublin, Odilo Globocnik, built camps in remote places on railway lines, staffed by a few dozen Germans, many of whom had gassed disabled people in the T4 'euthanasia' programme, and guards trained at Trawniki, mostly Soviet former prisoners. Chełmno, using gas vans, had begun killing in December 1941.

On 17 March 1942 deportations from the Lublin ghetto to Bełżec began. Sobibór started killing in May, and Treblinka in July, as the Warsaw ghetto was emptied. Trains arrived from Polish ghettos and later from across Europe. Victims were told they had reached a transit camp, made to undress and driven through a 'tube' into chambers filled with engine exhaust; within hours most were dead. Small groups of Jewish prisoners were forced to sort belongings and dispose of the bodies.

At the same time Auschwitz-Birkenau became a death camp with Zyklon B. Prisoners rose up at Treblinka in August 1943 and at Sobibór in October. The camps were then demolished, and some 42,000 remaining Jews in the Lublin district were shot in November 1943.
significance: The Reinhard camps carried out the destruction of Polish Jewry, the largest Jewish community in Europe; with Chełmno and Auschwitz they made murder an industrial process.
uncertaintyNote: Victim numbers rest largely on the intercepted Höfle telegram (over 1.27 million by the end of 1942), railway records and later investigations; figures for each camp vary between sources. The operation was named after Heydrich after his assassination in 1942.
sources: Yitzhak Arad, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka: The Operation Reinhard Death Camps (1987)
Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (3rd edn, 2003)
Saul Friedländer, The Years of Extermination (2007)

title: Indian Ocean raid
place: Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and the Bay of Bengal
casualties: British c. 1,000 seamen killed; a light carrier, 2 heavy cruisers, 2 destroyers and c. 23 merchant ships sunk; Japanese c. 20 aircraft lost
summary: Nagumo's carriers raid Ceylon, bomb Colombo and Trincomalee, and sink the carrier Hermes and two cruisers, driving the British Eastern Fleet back to East Africa.
detail:
With South-East Asia overrun, Japan sent five of the carriers that had attacked Pearl Harbor into the Indian Ocean. Warned by codebreakers and a Catalina flying boat, the British were waiting with Admiral Somerville's Eastern Fleet, whose old battleships and few carriers were no match for Nagumo.

On Easter Sunday, 5 April 1942, Japanese aircraft struck the harbour at Colombo, sinking an armed merchant cruiser and a destroyer; the same afternoon they found and sank the heavy cruisers Dorsetshire and Cornwall at sea, with the loss of over 400 men. On 9 April they hit the naval base at Trincomalee, and caught the small carrier Hermes and the Australian destroyer Vampire off the coast near Batticaloa, sinking both. Meanwhile a cruiser force under Ozawa sank some two dozen merchant ships in the Bay of Bengal, and aircraft bombed Vizagapatam and Cocanada on the Indian coast.

Somerville withdrew his fleet to Kilindini in Kenya. Nagumo, his raid accomplished, turned back to the Pacific.
significance: The raid marked the high-water mark of Japanese naval power in the west, spread panic along India's coast and prompted the British seizure of Madagascar, but Japan never returned in force.
uncertaintyNote: The position of the cruisers' sinking is approximate. Merchant ship losses in the Bay of Bengal vary slightly by source.
sources: Jonathan Parshall and Anthony Tully, Shattered Sword (2005)
Michael Tomlinson, The Most Dangerous Moment (1976)
Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, Forgotten Armies (2004)

title: Doolittle Raid
place: Tokyo, Yokohama, Nagoya, Kobe and Osaka, Japan

strength.opponent: 16 B-25 bombers flown from the carrier Hornet

casualties: c. 50 killed in Japan; all 16 aircraft lost, 3 airmen killed in crashes, 8 captured of whom 3 were executed; in Japanese reprisals in China c. 250,000 civilians died
summary: Sixteen army bombers take off from a carrier and strike Tokyo and other Japanese cities, a small raid that shocks Japan's leaders and brings savage reprisals on Chinese civilians.
detail:
Under Lieutenant-Colonel James Doolittle, sixteen twin-engined B-25s were loaded onto the carrier Hornet, escorted by Halsey's Enterprise. Spotted by a Japanese picket boat on the morning of 18 April 1942, the force launched early, some 650 miles from Japan. The bombers struck Tokyo, Yokohama, Yokosuka, Nagoya, Kobe and Osaka around midday, doing light damage and killing some fifty people, including children at a school in Tokyo.

None of the planes could land on the carrier, and with fuel running out they crash-landed or their crews bailed out over occupied China; one landed near Vladivostok and its crew was interned. Chinese villagers helped most of the airmen escape. Eight were captured by the Japanese, and three of them were executed after a show trial.

In revenge, Japanese armies swept through Zhejiang and Jiangxi provinces from May, destroying airfields and villages where the airmen had been sheltered; Unit 731 spread plague and other diseases. Chinese estimates put the dead at around 250,000.
significance: The raid lifted American morale and persuaded Japan's navy to press ahead with Yamamoto's plan to destroy the US fleet at Midway; its heaviest cost fell on Chinese civilians.
uncertaintyNote: The figure of about 250,000 Chinese deaths in the Zhejiang–Jiangxi reprisal campaign is a Chinese estimate and cannot be verified precisely. 'Defeat' here marks the raid as an Allied success; its military effect was small.
sources: James M. Scott, Target Tokyo (2015)
Craig Nelson, The First Heroes (2002)
Rana Mitter, China's War with Japan, 1937–1945 (2013)

title: Battle of the Coral Sea
place: Coral Sea, between New Guinea, the Solomons and Australia

strength.focus: 2 fleet carriers, 1 light carrier, c. 130 carrier aircraft

casualties: American c. 650 killed; carrier Lexington, a destroyer and an oiler sunk. Japanese c. 950 killed; light carrier Shōhō sunk, Shōkaku badly damaged, c. 90 aircraft lost
summary: In the first battle between aircraft carriers, fought without the fleets ever seeing each other, the US Navy turns back the Japanese seaborne invasion of Port Moresby.
detail:
Japan planned to seize Tulagi in the Solomons and Port Moresby in Papua, threatening the route between the United States and Australia. Codebreakers at Pearl Harbor read enough of the plan for Admiral Nimitz to send the carriers Lexington and Yorktown under Fletcher, with an Australian-American cruiser force under Crace.

After an American strike on Tulagi on 4 May, both sides searched for each other in poor weather. On 7 May US aircraft found and sank the light carrier Shōhō, covering the invasion convoy; Japanese aircraft sank the oiler Neosho and destroyer Sims, mistaken for a carrier. On 8 May the main carrier forces struck at each other simultaneously. Shōkaku was hit by three bombs and put out of action; Lexington took torpedoes and bombs, and that afternoon fuel vapour explosions tore through her and she was scuttled. Yorktown was damaged.

The Japanese commander, Admiral Inoue, recalled the Port Moresby invasion force. Japan would next try to reach the town overland, across the Owen Stanley Range.
significance: Coral Sea was a tactical draw but a strategic check: Japan's southward advance was halted for the first time, and two of its fleet carriers missed the decisive battle at Midway a month later.
uncertaintyNote: The Japanese sank a larger ship, so the battle is often called a tactical Japanese victory and a strategic Allied one; 'defeat' here reflects the strategic result. The central position is approximate.
sources: John B. Lundstrom, The First Team (1984)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
Jonathan Parshall and Anthony Tully, Shattered Sword (2005)

title: Fall of Corregidor
place: Corregidor island, mouth of Manila Bay, Philippines
casualties: American and Filipino c. 800 killed and c. 11,000–13,000 captured; Japanese c. 900 killed and wounded in the landings
summary: After weeks of bombardment, Japanese troops land on the island fortress of Corregidor and General Wainwright surrenders the last American forces in the Philippines.
detail:
Corregidor, a tadpole-shaped island guarding Manila Bay, had been MacArthur's headquarters and was the last stronghold once Bataan fell. Its garrison and thousands of refugees from Bataan lived in and around the Malinta tunnel, short of water and food. Through April Japanese artillery on Bataan and aircraft smashed the island's batteries and installations in one of the heaviest bombardments of the Pacific war.

On the night of 5 May Japanese troops crossed in landing barges. Many were killed in the water, but enough got ashore to hold a beachhead near the island's tail, and tanks followed. With the Japanese approaching the tunnel, crammed with wounded, General Jonathan Wainwright surrendered on 6 May. The Japanese insisted he order the surrender of all forces in the Philippines, which he did by radio; most units in the south complied in the following days, though some soldiers went to the hills and joined the guerrilla resistance.

Wainwright spent the rest of the war as a prisoner in Formosa and Manchuria.
significance: Corregidor's fall completed Japan's conquest of the Philippines, five months behind its original plan, and left the islands under an occupation that would be resisted by growing guerrilla movements.
uncertaintyNote: Prisoner figures for Corregidor alone are variously given between about 11,000 and 13,000.
sources: Louis Morton, The Fall of the Philippines (US Army official history, 1953)
Ronald H. Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
John Toland, The Rising Sun (1970)

title: Second Battle of Kharkov
place: South of Kharkov (Kharkiv), in the Izyum–Barvenkovo salient, Ukraine
casualties: Soviet c. 277,000, including c. 170,000 killed, missing or captured (Germans claimed c. 240,000 prisoners); German c. 20,000–30,000
summary: A Soviet spring offensive to retake Kharkov runs straight into German preparations for their own attack; the counter-stroke traps three Soviet armies south of the city.
detail:
Encouraged by the winter's successes, Stalin approved Marshal Timoshenko's plan to retake Kharkov, Ukraine's second city, with a pincer attack from the Volchansk area and from the Izyum salient, a bulge in the German line won in January. The offensive opened on 12 May 1942 and at first made good progress south of the city.

But the Germans were themselves preparing to pinch off the salient as a prelude to their summer offensive. On 17 May Kleist's army group struck its southern shoulder near Izyum. Timoshenko and his political commissar Nikita Khrushchev asked to call off the attack; Stalin, advised that the danger was exaggerated, refused until it was too late. On 22 May the Germans closed the neck of the salient, and over the next week the trapped armies were destroyed in repeated, desperate attempts to break out. Several Soviet army commanders, including Fyodor Kostenko, were killed.

The disaster left the southern front weak just as the German summer offensive was about to break.
significance: Second Kharkov destroyed the Soviet reserves in the south and opened the way for Germany's drive towards Stalingrad and the Caucasus in the summer of 1942.
uncertaintyNote: Soviet figures are Krivosheev's; the German prisoner claim was higher. Responsibility for the failure to halt the offensive was later disputed, notably by Khrushchev, who blamed Stalin.
sources: David M. Glantz, Kharkov 1942: Anatomy of a Military Disaster (1998)
David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
G. F. Krivosheev, ed., Soviet Casualties and Combat Losses in the Twentieth Century (1997)

title: Battle of Gazala and Bir Hakeim
place: The Gazala line, west of Tobruk, Libya

sides.opponent: Britain and the Commonwealth and Free France

casualties: British and Commonwealth c. 50,000 including prisoners, before the fall of Tobruk; Axis c. 30,000–35,000; Free French at Bir Hakeim c. 900 killed, wounded or captured
summary: Rommel swings round the southern end of the British Gazala line and, after a fierce battle in which the Free French hold Bir Hakeim for two weeks, routs Eighth Army.
detail:
Both sides were preparing to attack. Eighth Army held a line of minefields and fortified 'boxes' running south from Gazala on the coast to Bir Hakeim, held by the 1st Free French Brigade under Marie-Pierre Koenig. On the night of 26–27 May 1942 Rommel led his armour round Bir Hakeim into the British rear, while Italian infantry pinned the front.

The first days nearly went wrong for him: his tanks were cut off from supplies, short of fuel and trapped in an area called the Cauldron. But British counter-attacks were slow and piecemeal, and the Axis forces broke through the minefields to reopen a supply route, destroying a British brigade box on 1 June. Bir Hakeim held out against repeated attacks and bombing until the night of 10–11 June, when most of the garrison broke out. Rommel then defeated the British armour around the Knightsbridge box on 12–13 June, and on 14 June Ritchie ordered a retreat.

A week later, on 21 June, Tobruk fell with some 33,000 men.
significance: Gazala was Rommel's greatest victory, opening the way into Egypt; Bir Hakeim gave Free France a symbol of renewed fighting spirit.
uncertaintyNote: Casualty figures vary, especially as many British losses were prisoners; the fall of Tobruk on 21 June lies outside this event. Positions of Gazala and Bir Hakeim are approximate.
sources: Niall Barr, Pendulum of War: The Three Battles of El Alamein (2004)
I. S. O. Playfair, The Mediterranean and Middle East, vol. III (HMSO, 1960)
Jean-Louis Crémieux-Brilhac, La France Libre (1996)
